common_name: Golden Times Forsythia (Variegated Gold-and-Green Foliage Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in fertile, free-draining soil in a sheltered, partly shaded spot; hot afternoon sun can scorch the variegated leaves of Golden Times, so morning sun with midday relief keeps the foliage cleanest.

directions: Golden Times is grown chiefly for its narrow, finely toothed foliage rather than for a heavy flower show, though scattered bright yellow flowers still appear on bare wood in early to mid spring. New leaves emerge a strong solid gold, and as the season progresses many settle into green centers edged with a creamy white margin while some stems stay fully yellow, giving the whole bush a two-toned look distinct from any solid-green border forsythia. In autumn the foliage adds a third season of interest, shifting through pink, red, and purple tones before dropping. Site it out of the hottest midday sun to prevent leaf scorch, and prune by hand right after flowering rather than shearing, since shearing removes the patterned new growth that gives the cultivar its appeal.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Spectabilis Forsythia (Classic Large-Flowered Vase-Shaped Border Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Spectabilis is one of the oldest and most vigorous border forsythia selections, so give it full room to reach its mature vase shape rather than crowding it against other shrubs.

directions: Spectabilis is a long-established border forsythia selection prized for smothering its bare stems in dense, deep golden-yellow flowers from early to mid spring, ahead of the foliage, in a display generally considered heavier than many newer intermedia cultivars. It grows into a substantial, upright, vase-shaped shrub with arching branches, and its green summer leaves turn a muted purple-bronze in fall before dropping. Because it flowers on old wood, prune immediately after bloom, removing a portion of the thickest, oldest canes at ground level every few years to keep new flowering wood coming from the base. It adapts to a wide range of soils and needs little supplemental care once established, though full sun and even moisture give the fullest bloom.

common_name: Happy Centennial Forsythia (Extreme Cold-Hardy Compact Groundcover Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Happy Centennial was bred for extreme flower-bud cold hardiness, so it is a dependable choice in cold-winter regions where standard border forsythia often bloom poorly after a hard winter.

directions: Bred at a Canadian research station for gardens too cold to reliably flower most forsythia, Happy Centennial carries flower buds that shrug off temperatures near minus thirty degrees Fahrenheit, so it blooms heavily in light yellow along its bare stems even after severe winters that ruin the bud set on less hardy cultivars. Its low, wide, mounding habit stays well under three feet tall while spreading considerably wider, making it useful as a flowering groundcover or the front tier of a cold-climate shrub border rather than an upright specimen. Prune lightly right after flowering to control spread and remove any winter dieback. It tolerates a wide range of well-drained soils and needs little care once established beyond occasional renewal pruning of the oldest stems.

common_name: Sunrise Forsythia (Iowa State Cold-Hardy Mounding Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Sunrise was selected for cold hardiness in the northern Midwest, so it holds bud and flower well in USDA zone 3-4 gardens where marginal forsythia cultivars often disappoint.

directions: Sunrise was introduced by a Midwestern university breeding program specifically for gardens where winter cold routinely kills the flower buds of standard border forsythia, and it responds with a strong show of bright golden-yellow blooms along bare branches ahead of the leaves. It forms a broad, dense, mounding shrub with upright branching that stays reasonably tidy without heavy pruning, and its foliage develops an unusual deep maroon blush in autumn that is more pronounced than in most border forsythia. Prune right after flowering, thinning a few of the oldest stems to the ground every couple of years to keep the mound full and floriferous. It adapts to a range of soils and needs only routine watering once established.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

common_name: Festivus Gold Ninebark (Semi-Dwarf Bright Yellow Foliage Ninebark)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun; Festivus Gold holds its bright yellow color better in strong sun than many older golden ninebark selections, which tend to scorch or fade under the same exposure.

directions: Festivus Gold is a semi-dwarf ninebark selected for foliage that stays vividly yellow through the growing season, mellowing only slightly toward lime green by late summer, and it resists the leaf scorch and fungal spotting that plague many other gold-leaf ninebark cultivars in hot, sunny sites. Clusters of small white flowers open in late spring against the bright foliage, followed by reddish seed capsules, and older stems develop the peeling, layered bark typical of the genus. Its compact size fits foundation plantings and smaller borders where full-size golden ninebark would quickly need corralling. It tolerates both dry spells and periodic wet soil, and needs only occasional renewal pruning of the oldest canes at the base.

common_name: Auntie B Ninebark (Reblooming Orange-Red-to-Purple Foliage Ninebark)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to light shade; Auntie B was bred for a dense, compact, well-branched habit, so it needs less corrective pruning to stay tidy than older, looser ninebark cultivars.

directions: Auntie B emerged from a multi-generation Upper Midwest breeding program aimed at compact, healthy, colorful ninebark, and it stands out for new growth that opens small and orange-red before maturing to purple, plus notably better resistance to powdery mildew than many older dark-leaved selections. Unlike single-flush ninebark cultivars, it reliably produces a second round of blush-white flower clusters on vigorous current-season stems from midsummer into fall, on top of its normal late-spring bloom, and the ripening seed follicles can flush coral-pink to red in full sun. Its dense, mounded, well-branched habit needs relatively little corrective pruning to stay full and shapely. Grow in well-drained to moist soil in full sun for the best foliage color and heaviest rebloom.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to part shade; Panther grows narrower and more upright than most dark-leaved ninebark cultivars, so it fits tighter side-yard or vertical-accent spots that would crowd a wide-spreading selection like Diabolo.

directions: Panther is a patented ninebark selection valued for foliage that emerges an especially deep purple-black and holds that dark tone through summer heat better than many older dark-leaf cultivars. Its habit runs narrower and more upright than typical for the group, giving it a vertical presence useful as a thriller in mixed containers or a tight accent in the back of a border where a wide-spreading cultivar would not fit. Flat-topped clusters of pale pink-white flowers open on old wood in late spring, contrasting sharply with the near-black leaves, and reddish fruit capsules follow in fall. Grow in well-drained to moist soil in full sun for the darkest color, and remove a few of the oldest stems at the base every few years to renew growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to light shade; Luteus grows considerably larger than modern compact gold-leaf ninebark cultivars, so allow it room as a screen or informal hedge rather than a tight foundation spot.

directions: Luteus is one of the oldest golden-leaved ninebark selections still in cultivation, predating the more compact modern gold-leaf cultivars bred over the last few decades. New leaves emerge a clear golden yellow and gradually settle into chartreuse-green through the summer, giving a softer, looser color effect than newer, brighter selections. Small clusters of white to pale pink flowers open in late spring, followed by reddish seed capsules, and mature stems show the same peeling, multi-layered bark typical of the species. Because it grows considerably larger and more loosely than compact modern gold-leaf cultivars, it suits informal hedges, screens, or naturalized plantings better than a tight foundation bed, and it tolerates clay, drought, and a wide range of soil conditions once established.
